title: Model binding: layered pinning semantics and client migration playbook
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem statement:
Customers want deterministic control over which exact model artifact runs in production while retaining a simple API/SDK surface. We currently support multiple selector types across the stack (human-friendly tags, semver-like channels, and exact commit refs), but runtime resolution behavior is underspecified: who wins when multiple selectors are provided, how fallbacks occur across deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private), and how published performance profiles map to selected variants.

Goal:
1) Define a concise, unambiguous pinning semantics model that SDKs and the server honor.
2) Provide a documented client migration playbook so existing integrations can adopt layered pins without surprise rollouts.
3) Ensure performance profile attachments (published perf metadata) are tied to resolved artifacts and surfaced to Console and SDKs for optimization suggestions.

Non-goals:
- This ticket is not the implementation of the resolver in runtime; it is the contract and client-side behavior and tests.

Proposed semantics (layered precedence):
- ExplicitRef (highest precedence): an exact artifact identifier (commit hash / digest). When provided, resolver must return that artifact or fail fast if unavailable. No automatic fallback except via explicit fallbackRef field.
- ReleaseChannel (semver-like): a channel string (e.g., "1.18", "1.x", "latest-stable"). Semver ranges resolve to a pinned artifact chosen by the model publisher according to release window and stability rules. Resolver may map a channel to the latest artifact that satisfies the channel constraint at resolution time.
- PublisherTag (human tag): an opt-in tag created by the model publisher (e.g., "redwood-llama2-128b-perf-v2"). Tags are low-precedence and can be moved by the publisher; clients should treat tags as mutable pointers.
- DefaultAlias (lowest): account- or org-level default model alias (e.g., "recommended-text-embedding") used when no other selector is present.

Behavior rules and examples:
- Single-selector request: behave according to selector semantics above. If selector is ReleaseChannel or PublisherTag, return the current artifact and its published performance profile.
- Multi-selector request: clients may supply multiple selectors. Resolver applies precedence top-down: ExplicitRef > ReleaseChannel > PublisherTag > DefaultAlias. Example: {"explicit_ref":"sha256:abc123", "channel":"1.x"} -> returns explicit_ref.
- Fallbacks: to avoid silent drift, automatic fallback is only allowed for ReleaseChannel and PublisherTag and only to earlier compatible artifacts within the same channel; explicit_ref never falls back implicitly. Fallback policy is opt-in per-request via fields: "allow_fallback": "true" and "fallback_channels": ["1.17"].
- Timebound resolution: channel-to-artifact mapping is timeboxed with a resolution timestamp returned to clients. SDKs should cache resolved artifact for the TTL indicated (default 24h) and re-resolve after expiry.

Performance profile publishing contract:
- Every model artifact published to the catalog must include a performance_profile id that contains: median_latency_ms (95th percentile optional), avg_token_cost_usd, memory_bytes, recommended_batch_size, and quantization_compatibility_tags.
- The resolver response MUST include the resolved artifact id and the referenced performance_profile id; SDKs should hydrate and expose perf data to the application and Console.
- Migration: when a channel points at a new artifact, the perf_profile id may change: SDKs must surface both previous and current perf profiles in Console rollouts to allow cost/latency comparisons.

SDK surface proposals (examples):
- REST request body example:
  POST /v1/generate
  {
    "model_selector": {"channel": "1.x", "tag": "redwood-low-latency"},
    "pin_options": {"allow_fallback": false, "timeout_ms": 3000},
    "input": "..."
  }
- Client-side cache behavior:
  - On warm start, resolve model_selector -> {artifact_id, perf_profile_id, resolved_at, ttl_seconds}. Cache until resolved_at + ttl_seconds.
  - If request includes an explicit_ref, bypass cache.

Acceptance criteria (high level):
- Public contract RFC doc describing precedence, fallback flags, TTL semantics, and examples published in Confluence with approval from Runtime, SDK, and PM.
- SDK prototypes (JS + Python) implement client-side caching and respect explicit_ref semantics.
- Integration tests: resolver accepts multi-selector payloads and returns resolution metadata and perf_profile id.
- Console shows resolved artifact and perf profile for a sample canary traffic route.
- Migration playbook written and validated with Solutions Engineering on 2 internal test customers.

Out-of-scope (implementation specifics):
- Kernel selection or runtime scheduling changes based on perf profile; that is a follow-up after perf metadata consumption is stable.

References and links:
- Internal RFC draft: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INFR/Pinning+Semantics+Draft
- Example PR for SDK cache layer: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-js/pull/426
- Perf profile schema in proto: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folder/perf-profiles-schema

Risks / trade-offs:
- Strict explicit_ref semantics improve determinism but increase availability coupling; we must offer a clear fallback opt-in path to avoid customer outages when artifact is temporarily unavailable.
- Allowing mutable tags simplifies publisher UX but introduces drift; recommend default TTLs and Console alerts on tag moves.

Next steps:
1) Finalize RFC and get Runtime + SDK + PM signoff (this ticket).
2) Ship SDK prototypes that implement cache + resolve metadata (follow-up tickets will implement server fallback behavior).
3) Coordinate with Console to show perf_profile side-by-side during rollouts.
